introduction: Bahá’u’lláh’s command opens the guide: build houses of worship throughout the lands, and go to them at dawn. What follows is mostly letters about one such house in ‘Ishqábád and another in Chicago: who gave, who carried stones, how the design was chosen, why hospitals and schools belong beside the prayer hall. The outside voices come largely from earlier builders. Israel brings more than enough for the tabernacle, David is told it was well that the temple was in his heart, Ezra’s old men weep at the new foundation, and Nehemiah will not come down from the wall. The Qur’án speaks of the first sanctuary and of houses raised for remembrance at morn and evening. Others ask what a building can do. Jesus looks to a worship tied to no mountain and foretells that no stone will stand; Amos would rather have justice than songs; Dickinson keeps the Sabbath in an orchard, Blake finds a chapel where he used to play, and Tagore sends the worshipper out to the road-menders.
questions: The readings insist that “the outward Temple is also necessary,” while Jesus speaks of worship in spirit and in truth and Dickinson keeps the Sabbath at home. What can a shared building do that private devotion cannot, and the reverse?
A house of worship is to have a hospital, a hospice, a school and a university beside it. How do James, Ezekiel’s river from the sanctuary and Amos’s demand for justice bear on that plan?

“The consideration is not the amount but the love.” Set the widow’s mites, the poverty of the Macedonian churches and Wordsworth’s “give all thou canst” beside the gifts from Persian villages. What makes a gift large?

The design is settled by convention and majority vote, and all is to be “a means of unity.” What do Mill’s dissenting one and the reconciliation Jesus asks before the altar add to this picture of deciding together?

‘Abdu’l-Bahá calls the sweeper of the temple his master and asks to be servant rather than president. Where do the psalmist’s doorkeeper and Herbert’s sweeper agree with him, and what would change if a community believed it?

“This edifice shall be remembered eternally.” Jesus says no stone of the temple will be left on another, and Shelley’s king is forgotten beside his ruin. What, on these readings, is the part of a house of worship that lasts?

outside.why: “Blessed is he who, at the hour of dawn … directeth his steps” to the house of worship. The psalmist keeps the same hour: in the morning will I direct my prayer unto thee, and will look up.
A place of worship “for all the religionists of the world.” Isaiah hears the same of the temple in Jerusalem: mine house shall be called an house of prayer for all people.

All religions, races and sects under one shelter. The tenth Sikh Guru said it of the buildings themselves: the temple and the mosque are the same, and it is through error that people appear different.
“Its doors will be open to all the nations and all religions.” Solomon, dedicating his temple, prays for the stranger who is not of Israel and comes from a far country to pray there.
A House of Worship joined to a hospital, a hospice and a school for orphans. The Letter of James defines pure religion by the same company: the fatherless and widows in their affliction.
Worship with its “subsidiary branches” of healing and teaching. In Ezekiel’s vision a river runs out from the sanctuary, and the trees along it bear fruit for food and leaves for medicine.
“To make the heart of every one of you a temple.” Paul says it to the Corinthians as a fact about them: ye are the temple of God, and the Spirit of God dwelleth in you.

“The outward Temple is also necessary.” Jesus tells the woman of Samaria that the hour is coming when neither her mountain nor Jerusalem will be the place. If worship is in spirit and in truth, what is a building for?
The church as a house of covenant where different races and nations come together. Ephesians gives the image in stone: a middle wall of partition, broken down.
To praise God “clearly and openly” where the land is free. Daniel prays three times a day with his windows open toward Jerusalem where it is not, and after the decree is signed.

The reading hopes for open praise and public prayer. Jesus warns against prayer that is seen of men and sends the worshipper to a closet with the door shut. When does public worship help, and when does it tempt?
Remembrance of the Lord “in the early dawn.” The psalmist wakes his harp before the day: I myself will awake early.
Thanks for a house of worship established in a land. A psalm gives the worshipper’s own feeling for such a place: Lord, I have loved the habitation of thy house.
The house of worship will make “the fire of the love of God” surge forth. Leviticus asks of the altar what the reading hopes of the heart: the fire shall ever be burning; it shall never go out.

The melody of the friends rises, and they raise the anthem of praise. Amos hears God refuse the noise of songs and ask for judgment to run down as waters. What must go with the singing for it to be heard?

Teaching, a school on firm foundations, and devotions at dawn in one sentence. Simon the Just names three things on which the world stands: the Torah, the Temple service, and deeds of loving-kindness.
Dawning-points of remembrance “in every hamlet and city.” Malachi foresees worship no longer tied to one place: from the rising of the sun to its going down, in every place incense shall be offered.

The place of worship “supersedes all other” places of gathering. Emily Dickinson keeps the Sabbath staying at home, with a bobolink for a chorister and an orchard for a dome. What would she miss, and what does she see?

People should know the hour, gather, and pray in harmony. Justin Martyr describes the same custom about the year 155: on the day called Sunday all gather in one place, read, pray, and collect for orphans and widows.

Music is praised and hymns are to “enrapture the Concourse on High.” Augustine loved the singing in church and distrusted himself when the voice moved him more than the words. Is that a danger here too?
Verses chanted “in a most wondrous melody.” The last psalm calls for trumpet, psaltery, harp, timbrel, strings, organs and cymbals, and ends: let every thing that hath breath praise the Lord.
Notes about the building are to be published and circulated to encourage the builders. Habakkuk is told to write the vision plain upon tables, that he may run that readeth it.
A garden shining like a lamp, with pools and fountains “like unto the hearts of the lovers.” The Song of Solomon also speaks of love as a garden, with a spring and a fountain.
“First the planting of trees is necessary, then pruning and arranging.” Proverbs gives an order of work of the same kind: prepare thy work in the field, and afterwards build thine house.
The building is better standing in the middle of a flower garden. Bacon opens his essay on gardens with the reason: God Almighty first planted a garden, and it is the purest of human pleasures.

A garden may be made into a house of worship. In Blake’s poem a chapel has been built where he used to play on the green, and “Thou shalt not” is written over the door. What keeps a temple in a garden from becoming that chapel?
The first house in the West, before thousands. Zechariah, while the second temple was still a foundation, asks who hath despised the day of small things.
The house of worship is called the lodestone of divine confirmations. The psalm puts the dependence the other way round: except the Lord build the house, they labour in vain that build it.

A building raised for “communication between orient and occident.” Paul carries a collection from the Gentile churches to Jerusalem and explains it as a debt between peoples who have shared spiritual things.
To be built “with the utmost beauty and completeness.” Isaiah sees the fir, the pine and the box brought from Lebanon to beautify the place of the sanctuary.
A house of worship and then schools, kept up “even during the war years.” Nehemiah’s builders went on with the wall under threat: we made our prayer unto our God, and set a watch.
The Báb speaks of “the first house wherein the Book was revealed.” The Qur’án uses the same form of words for Mecca: the first sanctuary appointed for mankind, a blessed place.
“A secure sanctuary for all who humble themselves,” like the Ka‘bah. The Qur’án on that House: a resort for mankind and sanctuary, purified for those who bow and prostrate themselves.
Moses’s first institution was the tent he raised in the desert. The command for it in Exodus is one line: let them make me a sanctuary, that I may dwell among them.

The travelling tent is offered as the pattern for a temple. When David wants to replace it with a house of cedar, he is asked whether God ever requested one. What does a tent say that a temple cannot?
“The consideration is not the amount but the love.” Jesus says it of two mites thrown into the temple treasury by a widow who had nothing else.
A structure “founded on piety.” The phrase is the Qur’án’s, which prefers to a rival building the place of worship founded upon duty to God from the first day.

The friends, and an old man among them, carry the stones themselves. Nehemiah’s list of those who rebuilt Jerusalem keeps one bitter note: the nobles of Tekoa put not their necks to the work. Who is missing when a community builds?
Stones carried on the builders’ backs “with rejoicing.” When the foundation of the second temple was laid the people shouted for joy, while the old men who had seen the first house wept aloud.
Asked to be president of the body that will build, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá asks to be its servant. Jesus gives the rule: whosoever will be great among you shall be your minister.
The caretaker who sweeps the house of worship is called master. The psalmist would choose his post: I had rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God than to dwell in the tents of wickedness.
“This is not service, it is sovereignty.” George Herbert says the same of sweeping: who sweeps a room as for God’s laws makes that and the action fine.
Contributions from everywhere in Iran, “even from villages.” For the tabernacle in the wilderness they came, every one whose heart stirred him up and whose spirit made him willing.
Children in Khurasan give toward a temple in Chicago. In Luke the elders of Capernaum speak for a Roman officer: he loveth our nation, and he hath built us a synagogue.

“It was unheard of in the past for the East to lend its material support to the West.” Kipling’s line, written in 1889, says the two will never meet; the rest of his stanza allows one exception. Which half of it does this gift answer?
Help sent “despite being in utmost straitened circumstances.” Paul reports the same of the churches of Macedonia, whose deep poverty abounded unto the riches of their liberality.
An edifice that will rise “so high that it will be visible from a great distance.” Jesus’s figure for his hearers is a city set on an hill, which cannot be hid.
Letters to Persia are to be answered with joy, because the friends there rejoice to hear. Proverbs: as cold waters to a thirsty soul, so is good news from a far country.
A sum from Persia is carried by hand to the United States. Acts records the first such errand: the disciples sent relief, each according to his ability, by the hands of Barnabas and Saul.
“Numerous souls from the surrounding regions are contributing.” When Israel gave for the first temple the people rejoiced for that they offered willingly, and the king rejoiced with them.
A prayer for those who “expend what they have” for the house of worship. The Qur’án likens what is spent in God’s way to a grain that grows seven ears with a hundred grains in each.
Givers are prayed for, not thanked. David’s prayer over the temple offerings explains why: all things come of thee, and of thine own have we given thee.
A convention held to consult on the building. Proverbs: without counsel purposes are disappointed, but in the multitude of counsellors they are established.
Many plans have been drawn, and one must be chosen. Jesus asks which builder of a tower does not first sit down and count the cost, whether he have sufficient to finish it.
Architectural plans are compared at a convention. Moses is told to make the tabernacle after the pattern shewed to him in the mount, a plan not open to a vote.

“Whatever the Convention decides by majority vote is acceptable.” Mill holds that all mankind minus one would have no right to silence the one. What becomes of the delegate who still thinks the majority chose badly?
A decision carried out because the gathering made it. The council of Jerusalem sends out its ruling with the words: it seemed good unto us, being assembled with one accord.
“All matters must be made a means of unity.” Jesus puts concord before the offering itself: leave thy gift before the altar, and first be reconciled to thy brother.
Form and design are to be settled by consulting together. Proverbs: through wisdom is an house builded, and by understanding it is established.
The friends are to ask the Government for a site. The second temple began with a ruler’s leave: Cyrus king of Persia proclaims that the house may be built at Jerusalem.

“They are all good”: the choice among designs is left to the committee. Emerson says of the architect of St Peter’s that he builded better than he knew. How much of a sacred building is decided by its designers?
The Right of God comes first and gifts to the temple after. Jesus orders duties in the same way: these ought ye to have done, and not to leave the other undone.
A gift toward the repair of the house of worship, and a vow kept. King Joash set a chest at the temple gate for its repair, and the people rejoiced and cast in until there was money in abundance.
A woman has cut off her hair to give to the temple. Mary of Bethany anoints Jesus’s feet with costly ointment and wipes them with her hair, and the house is filled with the odour.

A small bequest may go to the house of worship or to “the poor of all religions”; either is acceptable. Some at Bethany were indignant that the ointment had not been sold for the poor. How does a community choose between the two?
“The contribution that thou hadst sent … has been received.” Paul acknowledges a gift from Philippi in the language of the altar: an odour of a sweet smell, a sacrifice acceptable.
“Out of this Mashriqu’l-Adhkár … thousands of Mashriqu’l-Adhkárs will be born.” Isaiah: a little one shall become a thousand, and a small one a strong nation.
“Soon shall that great Temple be completed.” Zechariah’s promise to the governor who began the second temple: his hands have laid the foundation of this house; his hands shall also finish it.
The joyful news that a house of worship is to be raised. A pilgrim psalm opens on the same gladness: I was glad when they said unto me, Let us go into the house of the Lord.
A desire “long cherished.” The psalmist’s soul longeth, yea, even fainteth for the courts of the Lord, where even the sparrow hath found an house.
“For each and every thing there is a prescribed season.” The Preacher’s list of seasons includes this one: a time to break down, and a time to build up.
To be erected “solidly and firmly.” Jesus’s wise man built his house upon a rock, and the rain, the floods and the winds did not bring it down.
“This edifice has a mighty effect upon the hearts.” Milton describes that effect in a cathedral: the high roof, the storied windows, the organ and the choir that bring all heaven before his eyes.
“God willing it shall be completed.” Paul’s confidence about the Philippians has the same ground: he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it.
The design of the first house is sent so that others may be drawn in its style. Hebrews recalls the charge to Moses: make all things according to the pattern shewed to thee.
Áqá Músá did not succeed in building during his lifetime. David was told the same about the temple, and something more: thou didst well that it was in thine heart.
The reading regrets what an unbuilt house might have done. Rabbi Tarfon’s saying takes the weight differently: it is not your duty to finish the work, but neither are you at liberty to neglect it.

Noble structures by the Jordan, “that the prophecies … may be fulfilled.” Amos is one such prophecy: in that day will I raise up the tabernacle of David that is fallen, and build it as in the days of old.

The first house is the mother, and its children will be reared “in glory, dignity, and utmost majesty.” Haggai promised the builders of a modest second temple that the glory of the latter house would be greater than of the former.
“Laying but one brick … is like unto building a lofty edifice.” Jesus gives the same measure to a cup of cold water: it shall in no wise lose its reward.
Opposition is foam on the shore; “be engaged” in the building. Nehemiah’s answer to those who wanted him off the wall: I am doing a great work, so that I cannot come down.
“If any disturbance arises they will prevent the construction.” So it happened to the second temple: its opponents wrote to the king that a rebellious city was being built, and the work ceased.
“The House itself will teach.” Habakkuk, in a darker setting, also lets a building speak: the stone shall cry out of the wall, and the beam out of the timber shall answer it.
Land has been bought, and nothing can yet be built on it. Thoreau thinks such work is not lost: if you have built castles in the air, now put the foundations under them. Is waiting part of building?
The land desired “is not available now but will be prepared in the future.” Hebrews honours those who died not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off.
The house where the Báb lived is “the most exalted of houses.” Jacob, waking where he had slept, says: this is none other but the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven.
A site is purchased. David, offered a threshing floor as a gift for his altar, insists on paying: neither will I offer unto the Lord of that which doth cost me nothing.
A dwelling is to become a place of worship because of who lived there. Moses is told at the bush: the place whereon thou standest is holy ground.

“How great is the endeavour! How sublime the undertaking!” Wordsworth defends the builder of King’s College Chapel against the charge of vain expense: give all thou canst; high Heaven rejects the lore of nicely-calculated less or more.
News that praise is now offered in a new house of worship. The psalm’s invitation: enter into his gates with thanksgiving, and into his courts with praise.
The Concourse on high hearkens and cries, “Happy are we.” Jesus speaks of the same listeners: there is joy in the presence of the angels of God.
Wealth spent “that they may remember Thee at dawn and at daybreak.” The Qur’án speaks of houses raised for God’s remembrance at morn and evening, and of those whom no merchandise distracts from it.

Wealth is spent on a building, and this is offered to God. Micah asks whether thousands of rams or rivers of oil are what is wanted, and answers: to do justly, and to love mercy. Can a building be an answer to Micah?
He spent “all that God had bestowed upon thee in this path.” The merchant of the parable finds one pearl of great price and sells all that he had to buy it.
Nine stones are laid on the chosen land and oil is poured on them. Jacob set up his stone pillow for a pillar and poured oil upon the top of it, and called the place Bethel, the house of God.

“That land is blessed because it is mentioned by the name” of what will stand there. Lincoln, dedicating a field, thought the words of the day mattered less than what had been done on the ground. What hallows a site?

A wish “to help carry earth” for the temple. Tagore tells the worshipper to leave the shut temple and find God where the tiller tills and the pathmaker breaks stones. Does carrying earth for a temple satisfy him?

“They were resented only because they chanted Thy verses.” The Qur’án speaks of those driven out only because they said, Our Lord is God, and of cloisters, churches, oratories and mosques defended together.
“This edifice shall be remembered eternally.” Shelley’s traveller finds a king’s boast carved on a ruin in an empty desert. What makes the difference between the two monuments?

The reading promises the building eternal remembrance. Jesus, shown the buildings of the temple by his disciples, says there shall not be left one stone upon another. Is it the stones that are to be remembered?

samuel-dwelt-in-a-tent.text: Shalt thou build me an house for me to dwell in? Whereas I have not dwelt in any house since the time that I brought up the children of Israel out of Egypt, even to this day, but have walked in a tent and in a tabernacle. In all the places wherein I have walked with all the children of Israel spake I a word with any of the tribes of Israel, whom I commanded to feed my people Israel, saying, Why build ye not me an house of cedar

chronicles-offered-willingly.text: Then the people rejoiced, for that they offered willingly, because with perfect heart they offered willingly to the Lord: and David the king also rejoiced with great joy

chronicles-of-thine-own.text: But who am I, and what is my people, that we should be able to offer so willingly after this sort? for all things come of thee, and of thine own have we given thee

exodus-make-me-a-sanctuary.text: And let them make me a sanctuary; that I may dwell among them

exodus-much-more-than-enough.text: The people bring much more than enough for the service of the work, which the Lord commanded to make. And Moses gave commandment, and they caused it to be proclaimed throughout the camp, saying, Let neither man nor woman make any more work for the offering of the sanctuary. So the people were restrained from bringing. For the stuff they had was sufficient for all the work to make it, and too much

ezra-shout-of-joy-and-weeping.text: And all the people shouted with a great shout, when they praised the Lord, because the foundation of the house of the Lord was laid. But many of the priests and Levites and chief of the fathers, who were ancient men, that had seen the first house, when the foundation of this house was laid before their eyes, wept with a loud voice; and many shouted aloud for joy: So that the people could not discern the noise of the shout of joy from the noise of the weeping of the people: for the people shouted with a loud shout, and the noise was heard afar off

kings-neither-hammer-nor-axe.text: And the house, when it was in building, was built of stone made ready before it was brought thither: so that there was neither hammer nor axe nor any tool of iron heard in the house, while it was in building

kings-stranger-from-a-far-country.text: Moreover concerning a stranger, that is not of thy people Israel, but cometh out of a far country for thy name's sake; (For they shall hear of thy great name, and of thy strong hand, and of thy stretched out arm;) when he shall come and pray toward this house; Hear thou in heaven thy dwelling place, and do according to all that the stranger calleth to thee for: that all people of the earth may know thy name, to fear thee, as do thy people Israel

psalm-awake-early.text: My heart is fixed, O God, my heart is fixed: I will sing and give praise. Awake up, my glory; awake, psaltery and harp: I myself will awake early

psalm-enter-into-his-gates.text: Enter into his gates with thanksgiving, and into his courts with praise: be thankful unto him, and bless his name

psalm-habitation-of-thy-house.text: Lord, I have loved the habitation of thy house, and the place where thine honour dwelleth

peter-lively-stones.text: Ye also, as lively stones, are built up a spiritual house, an holy priesthood, to offer up spiritual sacrifices, acceptable to God by Jesus Christ

ephesians-chief-corner-stone.text: And are built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone; In whom all the building fitly framed together groweth unto an holy temple in the Lord: In whom ye also are builded together for an habitation of God through the Spirit

mark-house-of-prayer-den-of-thieves.text: and Jesus went into the temple, and began to cast out them that sold and bought in the temple, and overthrew the tables of the moneychangers, and the seats of them that sold doves; And would not suffer that any man should carry any vessel through the temple. And he taught, saying unto them, Is it not written, My house shall be called of all nations the house of prayer? but ye have made it a den of thieves

matthew-not-one-stone-upon-another.text: And Jesus went out, and departed from the temple: and his disciples came to him for to shew him the buildings of the temple. And Jesus said unto them, See ye not all these things? verily I say unto you, There shall not be left here one stone upon another, that shall not be thrown down

luke-built-us-a-synagogue.text: And a certain centurion's servant, who was dear unto him, was sick, and ready to die. And when he heard of Jesus, he sent unto him the elders of the Jews, beseeching him that he would come and heal his servant. And when they came to Jesus, they besought him instantly, saying, That he was worthy for whom he should do this: For he loveth our nation, and he hath built us a synagogue

corinthians-deep-poverty-abounded.text: Moreover, brethren, we do you to wit of the grace of God bestowed on the churches of Macedonia; How that in a great trial of affliction the abundance of their joy and their deep poverty abounded unto the riches of their liberality. For to their power, I bear record, yea, and beyond their power they were willing of themselves; Praying us with much intreaty that we would receive the gift, and take upon us the fellowship of the ministering to the saints

romans-contribution-for-the-poor-saints.text: But now I go unto Jerusalem to minister unto the saints. For it hath pleased them of Macedonia and Achaia to make a certain contribution for the poor saints which are at Jerusalem. It hath pleased them verily; and their debtors they are. For if the Gentiles have been made partakers of their spiritual things, their duty is also to minister unto them in carnal things

acts-every-man-according-to-his-ability.text: Then the disciples, every man according to his ability, determined to send relief unto the brethren which dwelt in Judaea: Which also they did, and sent it to the elders by the hands of Barnabas and Saul

chronicles-cast-into-the-chest.text: And at the king's commandment they made a chest, and set it without at the gate of the house of the Lord. And they made a proclamation through Judah and Jerusalem, to bring in to the Lord the collection that Moses the servant of God laid upon Israel in the wilderness. And all the princes and all the people rejoiced, and brought in, and cast into the chest, until they had made an end. Now it came to pass, that at what time the chest was brought unto the king's office by the hand of the Levites, and when they saw that there was much money, the king's scribe and the high priest's officer came and emptied the chest, and took it, and carried it to his place again. Thus they did day by day, and gathered money in abundance

genesis-jacob-set-up-a-pillar.text: And Jacob rose up early in the morning, and took the stone that he had put for his pillows, and set it up for a pillar, and poured oil upon the top of it. And he called the name of that place Bethel

proverbs-prepare-thy-work-without.text: Prepare thy work without, and make it fit for thyself in the field; and afterwards build thine house

proverbs-through-wisdom-is-an-house-buil.text: Through wisdom is an house builded; and by understanding it is established: And by knowledge shall the chambers be filled with all precious and pleasant riches

nehemiah-i-am-doing-a-great-work.text: That Sanballat and Geshem sent unto me, saying, Come, let us meet together in some one of the villages in the plain of Ono. But they thought to do me mischief. And I sent messengers unto them, saying, I am doing a great work, so that I cannot come down: why should the work cease, whilst I leave it, and come down to you

nehemiah-nobles-put-not-their-necks.text: And next unto them the Tekoites repaired; but their nobles put not their necks to the work of their Lord

zechariah-hands-shall-also-finish-it.text: The hands of Zerubbabel have laid the foundation of this house; his hands shall also finish it; and thou shalt know that the Lord of hosts hath sent me unto you

philippians-begun-a-good-work.text: Being confident of this very thing, that he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ

samuel-that-which-doth-cost-me-nothing.text: And the king said unto Araunah, Nay; but I will surely buy it of thee at a price: neither will I offer burnt offerings unto the Lord my God of that which doth cost me nothing. So David bought the threshingfloor and the oxen for fifty shekels of silver

proverbs-honour-the-lord-with-thy-substa.text: Honour the Lord with thy substance, and with the firstfruits of all thine increase: So shall thy barns be filled with plenty, and thy presses shall burst out with new wine

habakkuk-stone-shall-cry-out.text: For the stone shall cry out of the wall, and the beam out of the timber shall answer it

job-morning-stars-sang-together.text: Where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth? declare, if thou hast understanding. Who hath laid the measures thereof, if thou knowest? or who hath stretched the line upon it? Whereupon are the foundations thereof fastened? or who laid the corner stone thereof; When the morning stars sang together, and all the sons of God shouted for joy

luke-joy-in-the-presence-of-the-angels.text: Likewise, I say unto you, there is joy in the presence of the angels of God over one sinner that repenteth

ecclesiastes-observeth-the-wind.text: He that observeth the wind shall not sow; and he that regardeth the clouds shall not reap

genesis-planted-a-garden.text: And the Lord God planted a garden eastward in Eden; and there he put the man whom he had formed. And out of the ground made the Lord God to grow every tree that is pleasant to the sight, and good for food; the tree of life also in the midst of the garden, and the tree of knowledge of good and evil. And a river went out of Eden to water the garden; and from thence it was parted, and became into four heads

isaiah-beautify-the-place-of-my-sanctuar.text: The glory of Lebanon shall come unto thee, the fir tree, the pine tree, and the box together, to beautify the place of my sanctuary; and I will make the place of my feet glorious

quran-first-sanctuary.text: Lo! the first Sanctuary appointed for mankind was that at Becca, a blessed place, a guidance to the peoples;

quran-raising-the-foundations.text: And when Abraham and Ishmael were raising the foundations of the House, (Abraham prayed): Our Lord! Accept from us (this duty). Lo! Thou, only Thou, art the Hearer, the Knower.

quran-places-of-worship-are-for-allah.text: And the places of worship are only for Allah, so pray not unto anyone along with Allah.

quran-place-of-resort-and-sanctuary.text: And when We made the House (at Makka) a resort for mankind and sanctuary, (saying): Take as your place of worship the place where Abraham stood (to pray). And We imposed a duty upon Abraham and Ishmael, (saying): Purify My house for those who go around and those who meditate therein and those who bow down and prostrate themselves (in worship).

wordsworth-give-all-thou-canst.text: TAX not the royal Saint with vain expense, / With ill-matched aims the Architect who planned— / Albeit labouring for a scanty band / Of white robed Scholars only—this immense / And glorious Work of fine intelligence! / Give all thou canst; high Heaven rejects the lore / Of nicely-calculated less or more
wordsworth-give-all-thou-canst.author: William Wordsworth
wordsworth-give-all-thou-canst.work: Inside of King’s College Chapel, Cambridge

milton-dim-religious-light.text: But let my due feet never fail, / To walk the studious Cloysters pale, / And love the high embowed Roof, / With antick Pillars massy proof, / And storied Windows richly dight, / Casting a dimm religious light. / There let the pealing Organ blow, / To the full voic'd Quire below, / In Service high, and Anthems cleer, / As may with sweetnes, through mine ear, / Dissolve me into extasies, / And bring all Heav'n before mine eyes
milton-dim-religious-light.author: John Milton
milton-dim-religious-light.caveat: The spelling is that of the early editions.

emerson-builded-better-than-he-knew.text: The hand that rounded Peter's dome / And groined the aisles of Christian Rome / Wrought in a sad sincerity; / Himself from God he could not free; / He builded better than he knew;— / The conscious stone to beauty grew
emerson-builded-better-than-he-knew.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
